atlas-kw.0047: KPC hires fresh graduates in non-engineering and non-science majors through announced campaigns restricted to Kuwaiti nationals, with a two-year onboarding programme; engineering and science graduates apply through Kuwait Oil Company or Kuwait National Petroleum Company.
atlas-kw.0048: Of the 495,697 Kuwaitis employed on 30 June 2026, 80.1% worked for the government; the private sector is 96.4% non-Kuwaiti, and unemployment among Kuwaiti citizens was 6.45% against 0.18% for expatriates.
atlas-kw.0049: IT roles open to foreigners are advertised mostly for experienced staff, with visa sponsorship; there is no graduate pipeline for non-nationals.
atlas-kw.0050: Zain Kuwait’s “Technical Opportunities for Recent Graduates” posting (closing date 28 February 2026) asked for a bachelor’s in MIS, engineering, telecom engineering or computer science, some internship exposure and a copy of Kuwaiti nationality from Sahel.
atlas-kw.0051: There is no national season for foreign hires: employers recruit when a post opens, KPC opens campaigns only when it announces them, and the visa takes about 4 to 8 weeks after an offer.
atlas-kw.0052: The programmes read ask for a bachelor’s (KIA: awarded within three years, GPA of 3.00 and a GMAT score); none requires a master’s. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0053: Kuwait is not party to the Hague Apostille Convention: a foreign degree needs the traditional consular legalisation chain, and the Ministry of Higher Education issues the equivalence certificate (Moadala); Law 78 of 2019 punishes use of unrecognised foreign degrees with up to five years in prison. Engineers are verified through the ministry and the Public Authority for Manpower.
atlas-kw.0054: The programmes read set a GPA of 3.00 or higher (KIA) and accredited institutions (Ministry of Higher Education); we found no ranking of schools by employers. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0055: We found no apprenticeship or dual-study route into graduate jobs; the library finds no internship visa for foreigners. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0056: 80.1% of employed Kuwaitis (397,165 of 495,697) worked in the public sector on 30 June 2026, but it is almost entirely closed to foreigners.
atlas-kw.0057: Foreign staff are 96.4% of the private-sector workforce, so private employers do sponsor, but entry-level expatriate hiring is the first target of the localisation policy and each work permit needs a Public Authority for Manpower approval and a 150 KWD recruitment fee. See Visas for the rules.
atlas-kw.0058: Zain Kuwait’s graduate application asks for a CV, a passport-size photograph, the highest qualification and a copy of the Civil ID or passport; this is one employer’s form.
atlas-kw.0059: No page we read states a CV length for Kuwait; we assume the regional default of up to two pages. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0060: The Zain, KIA and KPC application flows read run on an online portal with tests and a form, with no cover letter mentioned. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0061: None of the application pages read asks for references up front; KPC makes its offer conditional on pre-employment requirements under Kuwaiti labour law. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0062: The library’s guide asks for the degree and a police-clearance certificate (issued within three months) translated into Arabic and legalised through the consular chain, with the Foreign Ministry stamp in Kuwait; the work contract must be in Arabic, with a translation allowed.
atlas-kw.0063: None of the application pages read asks for a salary expectation; the contract states salary in KWD, allowances and notice terms. We did not establish how often recruiters ask. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0064: The state does the checking for a foreign hire: a legalised police-clearance certificate, a medical screening at the Ministry of Health and fingerprints at the Interior Ministry before residence is issued; KPC adds pre-employment requirements for nationals.
atlas-kw.0065: Personal recommendation (wasta) and recruiters carry most hiring.
atlas-kw.0066: A foreign hire can be recruited from abroad: the employer files the Public Authority for Manpower approval and the Interior Ministry entry visa (3 to 5 weeks), then the medical, fingerprints and Civil ID follow in Kuwait within 60 days of entry; no work or internship can start on a visit visa.
atlas-kw.0067: The contract language is Arabic by law, with a translation allowed; KIA asks for proficiency in Arabic and English. For foreign staff in banks and multinationals English is the working language, but no source measured it. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0068: KPC’s fresh-graduate process has five stages: an announced campaign, a preliminary review, assessment tests, a personal interview and a conditional offer after pre-employment checks; the page gives no timing, test format or language. KIA applicants who meet the requirements take an assessment test on finance, accounting and economics.
atlas-kw.0069: Zain Kuwait’s graduate application starts with account registration and uploads of a CV, photograph, qualification and ID copies. These are the nationals’ flows; we found no page describing interviews, assessment centres or dress norms for foreign graduates.
atlas-kw.0070: Rivermate (6 August 2026): probation is at most 100 working days and cannot be repeated for the same role, and either party can end the contract in it without notice; notice is generally three months for monthly-paid staff; end-of-service pay starts after one year at 15 days’ salary per year for the first five years, then one month per year.
atlas-kw.0071: A written contract is mandatory and its official language is Arabic, with a translation allowed; it states duties, workplace, salary in KWD, allowances, hours, leave and notice. The guide gives a 48-hour week, 36 in Ramadan, and 30 paid days of annual leave after six months, but is inconsistent on hours, so verify. The employer pays the recruitment fee, visa, residence and medical costs. We did not establish whether graduates negotiate or how long employers give to decide.
atlas-kw.0072: The employer needs an active file with the Public Authority for Manpower, a Kuwaitisation quota in good standing and prior approval to recruit from abroad; the recruitment fee is 150 KWD per new permit and the library counts about 305 KWD of first-year government costs, all on the employer. Fines for missing Kuwaitisation targets were reported in 2024 as set to rise from 100 to 300 KWD, with proposed rates of 50% in oil and about 30% in other sectors.
atlas-kw.0073: Because the private sector is 96.4% non-Kuwaiti, employers do hire foreigners, but the state is pressing them to replace expatriates where Kuwaitis could do the job, and a 2026 legal guide says banks must keep at least 70% Kuwaiti staff and other sectors between 1% and 30%, without dating it. Ask early who sponsors, which entity employs you and whether the post is inside a quota. This is our reading for the last point.
atlas-kw.0074: Employer portals: KPC’s recruitment portal (recruitment.kpc.com.kw), the Kuwait Investment Authority’s portal (portal.kia.gov.kw) and Zain Kuwait’s careers site (careers.zain.com); all three are for Kuwaiti graduates. We could not open the pages of the Big Four, KOC or the other banks.
atlas-kw.0075: Fairs and universities: the Australian University (AU) in Kuwait’s fair, Kuwait University’s fair and the Career Fair at the Kuwait International Fair; the Public Authority for Manpower, which was a silver sponsor at the 2022 AU fair, supervises work permits and quotas.
atlas-kw.0076: Applying to the national programmes (KIA, KPC campaigns, NBK Academy, the central bank’s programme, Zain’s graduate posting) as a foreign graduate: they require Kuwaiti nationality.
atlas-kw.0077: Starting an internship or trial work on a visit or tourist visa: the library says it is illegal work, with arrest, detention and expulsion with a ban across the Gulf states.
atlas-kw.0078: Relying on an Apostille: Kuwait is not party to the Hague Convention, so a degree or police certificate with only an Apostille is rejected and needs the consular chain.
atlas-kw.0079: Handing over your passport to the employer: the library notes the law bans employers from keeping it without written consent, yet many ask; do not give it up without a formal receipt.
atlas-kw.0080: Missing the 60-day deadline after entry to finish residence: the library cites daily fines of 2 KWD in the first month and 4 KWD after, up to 1,200 KWD.
atlas-kw.0081: The Kuwait Investment Authority asks its Kuwaiti applicants for proficiency in Arabic and English in reading, writing and conversation; we found no bank page stating a level for foreign graduates.
atlas-kw.0082: Employment contracts must be in Arabic by law, with a translation allowed, and Rivermate notes that local graduates are often fluent in both Arabic and English. For foreign staff in multinationals English is the working language, but no source measured it. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0083: Government posts are almost entirely reserved for Kuwaiti citizens, so Arabic is the working language there; no page gave a level. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0084: Zain Kuwait’s graduate posting asks for strong communication skills and does not state a language level; IT roles for foreigners are mostly for experienced staff. This is our reading.
atlas-kw.0085: On 30 June 2026 unemployment among Kuwaiti citizens was 6.45% (31,794 people, up from 6.2% at the end of 2025) against 0.18% for expatriates. We found no graduate-specific figure, return-offer rate or time to first job for Kuwait.
